C2 beacon to audit.checkmarx[.]cx /v1/telemetry (TeamPCP Shai-Hulud Third Coming) AICommand & Control High
Detects any outbound network/DNS activity to the TeamPCP C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx (94.154.172.43) — particularly POSTs to the /v1/telemetry path — that exfiltrates harvested cloud, CI/CD and developer credentials from compromised hosts. The domain visually impersonates Checkmarx's legitimate infrastructure but resolves to attacker-controlled space. Rationale: Article Table 1 names the C2 server, IP and HTTP path explicitly (audit.checkmarx[.]cx:443 / 94.154.172.43 / /v1/telemetry) — any hit on these three indicators is a confirmed-compromise signal, not a hunting hypothesis. Corroborated by Checkmarx's official disclosure that all four artifact families (npm, Docker Hub, GitHub Actions, VS Code) shared this C2. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually visiting the domain during IR triage (filter on known analyst workstation/jump-host)
  • Threat-intel sandbox or scanner deliberately resolving the IOC (e.g. a TI enrichment service hosted on the corporate network)
  • Outbound proxy/DLP solution generating a synthetic resolution for the indicator feed
  • Endpoint EDR sensor itself pulling the indicator for local matching (filter on MsSense.exe / SenseIR.exe)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-jump-01","ir-analyst-vm")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull every host that resolved audit.checkmarx[.]cx or connected to 94.154.172.43 in the last 30 days; for each, identify the initiating process and user. Capture the full HTTPS request body if proxy decryption is available — POST to /v1/telemetry carries exfiltrated tokens. Step 2 — Contain: Block audit.checkmarx[.]cx and 94.154.172.43 at DNS, proxy and firewall. Force-rotate every npm token, GitHub PAT, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI credential, Docker Hub token and .env-stored secret on every connecting host within the last 24h. Step 3 — Hunt: For each affected user, list every npm package and GitHub repo they own — TeamPCP's worm republishes packages and creates public 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' repos under the victim identity. Pivot to UC #3 (file artifacts) and UC #1 (Bun download).
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx", "audit.checkmarx[.]cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (c2Hosts)) or (RemoteIP in (c2Ips)) or (RemoteUrl has c2Path and RemotePort in (443, 80))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstHostname has_any (c2Hosts) or DstIpAddr in (c2Ips) or (isnotempty(Url) and Url has c2Path and DstPortNumber in (443, 80))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
),
(
  ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (c2Hosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseCodeName
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or Url has c2Path and (HttpHostName has "checkmarx.cx")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or DestinationIP in (c2Ips) or RequestURL has "audit.checkmarx.cx" or RequestURL has c2Path
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP Shai-Hulud C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx Connection
id: 7e5a3b2c-1f4d-4a6e-9b8f-3c2d1e4f5a62
status: experimental
description: Detects connections or DNS resolutions to the TeamPCP / Shai-Hulud Third Coming C2 infrastructure (audit.checkmarx[.]cx / 94.154.172.43) used by the @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm supply-chain payload and the broader Checkmarx-distribution-channel compromise to exfiltrate harvested credentials via /v1/telemetry.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_domain:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'audit.checkmarx.cx'
  selection_ip:
    QueryResults|contains:
      - '94.154.172.43'
  condition: selection_domain or selection_ip
falsepositives:
  - None expected; the domain is attacker-controlled and not Checkmarx's real infrastructure (legitimate Checkmarx uses checkmarx.com / checkmarx.net).
level: critical
(@network.destination.domain:audit.checkmarx.cx OR CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 94.154.172.43/32) OR @http.url:*audit.checkmarx.cx* OR @http.url:*/v1/telemetry* OR @dns.question.name:*audit.checkmarx.cx*)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/audit\.checkmarx\.cx/i)
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="94.154.172.43")
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6 (RemoteAddressIP6=*94.154.172.43* OR ContextImageFileName=/(node|bun|npm)/i AND RemotePort=443))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
(`cim_Network_Traffic_indexes` (dest="audit.checkmarx.cx" OR dest="audit.checkmarx[.]cx" OR dest_ip="94.154.172.43")) OR (`cim_Network_Resolution_indexes` query="*audit.checkmarx.cx*") OR (`cim_Web_indexes` (url="*audit.checkmarx.cx*" OR dest="audit.checkmarx.cx") (url="*/v1/telemetry*" OR uri_path="/v1/telemetry")) | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count by host src dest dest_ip url http_method app | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Malicious @bitwarden/cli payload artifacts on disk (bw_setup.js, bw1.js, Shai-Hulud markers) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or execution of the Stage-1 (bw_setup.js) and Stage-2 (bw1.js) Node.js scripts dropped by the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm package, as well as the 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' string written into public repo content that the worm uses as an attribution marker and propagation beacon. This catches both the install-time drop on the npm install path and any post-compromise replay. Rationale: Article explicitly names bw_setup.js (Stage-1 bootstrap, registered as the `bw` bin) and bw1.js (Stage-2 Bun payload) inside the malicious @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 package. The legitimate Bitwarden CLI ships neither filename, so the filename + package path combo is a hard-IOC match. The Shai-Hulud Third Coming string is a TeamPCP attribution marker per the article body. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://github.com/bitwarden/clients/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher unzipping a captured copy of the malicious package on an analyst workstation for analysis (filter on known analyst hosts)
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline downloading the package from npm cache for IOC extraction
  • SOC sandbox/detonation environment replaying the package install
  • Legitimate package named 'bw1.js' or 'bw_setup.js' shipped by an unrelated internal project (unlikely; verify against package.json)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\sandboxes\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\detonation\\" and DeviceName !startswith "ti-sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "malware-analysis-"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Capture the dropping process tree and the surrounding package.json — confirm version is 2026.4.0 and that the preinstall script invokes bw_setup.js. Hash bw1.js and submit to threat intel. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate host, run `npm uninstall -g @bitwarden/cli` and `npm cache clean --force`, wipe ~/.npm/_cacache, kill any lingering bun.exe / node.exe processes parented by npm, rotate all credentials reachable from the host (npm token, GitHub PAT, cloud CLI tokens, .env secrets, SSH keys). Step 3 — Hunt: Query the user's GitHub for any new public repository created in the last 30 days containing the string 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' — this is the worm's propagation marker — and audit every npm package the user can publish for unauthorised releases.
let stageFiles = dynamic(["bw_setup.js", "bw1.js"]);
let packageHints = dynamic(["@bitwarden\\cli", "@bitwarden/cli", "node_modules\\@bitwarden\\cli", "node_modules/@bitwarden/cli"]);
let shaiHuludMarker = "Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (FileName in~ (stageFiles)) or (FolderPath has_any (packageHints) and FileName endswith ".js") or (AdditionalFields has shaiHuludMarker)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName, SHA256;
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (stageFiles)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName = FileName, SHA256, ProcCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let stageFiles = dynamic(["bw_setup.js", "bw1.js"]);
let packageHints = dynamic(["@bitwarden\\cli", "@bitwarden/cli", "node_modules\\@bitwarden\\cli", "node_modules/@bitwarden/cli"]);
let npmRunners = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","bun"]);
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where (TargetFileName in~ (stageFiles)) or (TargetFilePath has_any (packageHints) and TargetFileExtension =~ "js")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256;
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (npmRunners) or ParentProcessName has_any (npmRunners)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (stageFiles)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              TargetFilePath = "", TargetFileName = "", TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

level: high

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Unauthenticated access to MantisBT admin/install.php on a production host (CVE-2026-52847) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Credential-phishing form injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) · [LLM] Meta open-redirect injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Broad reflected HTML/XSS payload tokens in MantisBT install.php query string · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated access to MantisBT admin/install.php on a production host (CVE-2026-52847) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts for HTTP requests that reach /admin/install.php with a 200 response after deployment. The installer should be removed/restricted post-install; its continued reachability is both the precondition for the reflected-XSS chain and a recon signal. Rationale: Uses the exact installer path /admin/install.php named in the advisory plus a 200-status filter; the installer's reachability is the stated precondition for the whole XSS chain and the workaround is to remove /admin. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory DB entry for CVE-2026-52847. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin performing an in-place upgrade or fresh install of MantisBT
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring configured to hit the app root that redirects into the installer
  • DevOps CI pipeline validating a freshly deployed MantisBT container
  • Security team running an authorized pentest against the tracker
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is not an authorized admin/scanner and whether the MantisBT version is <=2.28.3. Review the csUriQuery values returned for injected HTML tokens (form/meta). Step 2 (contain): Remove or ACL-restrict the /admin directory per the vendor workaround, or upgrade to 2.28.4+; block external access to /admin/install.php at the WAF/reverse proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same source IP across web logs for other admin-path probing and for follow-on requests carrying reflected-XSS payloads (see the form-injection and meta-redirect UCs).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where scStatus == 200
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Queries = make_set(csUriQuery, 20) by cIP, csUriStem, csMethod, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by Hits desc

Credential-phishing form injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP requests to /admin/install.php whose query string carries injected <form>/action markup — the credential-phishing primitive the advisory calls out, enabled by the missing CSP form-action directive. The payload is reflected from user-supplied parameters via print_test_result(). Rationale: Targets the advisory's explicit 'credential-phishing form injection' primitive using the concrete injector path /admin/install.php and injected <form action=...> tokens (both raw and URL-encoded). The missing form-action CSP directive means the injected form is the actual exploitation vector, making these tokens high-fidelity. Confirmed via GitLab CVE-2026-52881 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1189 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester/bug-bounty tester replaying the watchTowr PoC against the tracker
  • A generic web vulnerability scanner (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) firing XSS templates that include <form> payloads
  • A legitimate query parameter that coincidentally contains the literal string 'action=http' (e.g. a callback/return URL param)
  • WAF audit-mode traffic replaying attack corpora
Suppression filter
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction") // require an actual form tag, not just action=http return-URL params
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the csUriQuery and confirm an injected <form> with an action pointing off-host; note the target action domain as attacker credential-harvest infra. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP and the harvest domain at the WAF/proxy, and restrict/remove /admin/install.php or upgrade to MantisBT 2.28.4+. Step 3 (hunt): Search web logs for any admin sessions or credential POSTs to the identified harvest domain, and pivot on the source IP for the meta-redirect variant and installer-probe activity.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction", "form%20action", "action=http", "action%3Dhttp", "method=post", "method%3Dpost")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Meta open-redirect injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) AIDelivery High
Detects requests to /admin/install.php whose reflected query string contains injected <meta http-equiv=refresh> markup — the open-redirect primitive the advisory describes, also enabled by the absent CSP form-action directive. Redirects victims silently to phishing/malware. Rationale: Targets the advisory's explicit '<meta> open redirects' primitive, requiring both an injected <meta> token and a refresh/http-equiv/url= token on the exact /admin/install.php path so it fires only on the redirect-injection shape, not generic meta references. Confirmed via GitLab CVE-2026-52881 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester replaying the watchTowr open-redirect PoC
  • Automated scanner (Nuclei/ZAP) firing open-redirect templates containing <meta refresh>
  • A legitimate parameter carrying a 'url=http...' return address that coincidentally sits near a meta reference
  • WAF corpus replay in audit mode
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode csUriQuery, extract the redirect target URL from the injected <meta ... url=> and check it against threat intel. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP and redirect-target domain at the WAF/proxy; remove/restrict /admin/install.php or upgrade to 2.28.4+. Step 3 (hunt): Look for users who subsequently connected to the redirect-target domain (proxy/DNS logs) and correlate with the same source IP's form-injection or probe activity.

| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<meta", "%3Cmeta")
| where csUriQuery has_any ("http-equiv", "refresh", "url=http", "url%3Dhttp")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Broad reflected HTML/XSS payload tokens in MantisBT install.php query string AIExploitation Medium
Hunting-tier catch-all for any HTML-injection markup reflected through /admin/install.php's six unescaped print_test_result() parameters. Broader than the targeted form/meta rules — surfaces CSS-injection UI-manipulation and event-handler probing that the tighter alerting rules miss. Rationale: Ties any HTML-markup token to the specific vulnerable path /admin/install.php named in the advisory; scoping the broad angle-bracket/event-handler net to this one endpoint keeps it deployable while catching CSS-injection UI manipulation and probing the two alerting rules don't cover. The endpoint anchor is what makes this article-specific rather than a generic WAF signature. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

MantisBT self-registration (signup.php) followed by SOAP replay to mantisconnect.php from same source AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-47156 exploitation path: an attacker self-registers via signup.php then immediately drives the SOAP API (/api/soap/mantisconnect.php) using the auth-bypass to impersonate the administrator. Flags a single source IP that touches the self-registration page and the SOAP endpoint within a short window — the article-specific signup-to-SOAP pivot. Rationale: Uses the two concrete URIs from the attack chain — signup.php (default self-registration, $g_allow_signup=ON) and /api/soap/mantisconnect.php (the SOAP endpoint) — correlated by source IP inside 30 min. Legit SOAP integrations authenticate with pre-provisioned service accounts and never register, so signup→SOAP from one IP is high-fidelity for CVE-2026-47156. Cross-checked watchTowr credit and the MantisBT 2.28.4 advisory confirming the endpoint and default self-registration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-47156/ • https://mantisbt.org/blog/archives/mantisbt/846 • https://mantisbt.org/blog/archives/mantisbt/852 • https://mantisbt.org/docs/master-1.3.x/en-US/Admin_Guide/html/admin.config.soap.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate new user self-registers and their team's SOAP integration client shares the same NAT/egress IP
  • Security scanner (Nessus/Qualys) crawling both the signup page and the SOAP WSDL from one IP
  • Internal QA/staging test harness that registers a throwaway account then exercises the SOAP API
  • Shared corporate proxy where many users egress from one IP, coincidentally overlapping signup and SOAP traffic
Suppression filter
| where NOT (uris IN ("/scanner/*")) // exclude known vuln-scanner paths; add your integration egress IPs to an allowlist lookup and filter with `| search NOT [| inputlookup mantis_soap_allowlist.csv | fields src]`
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the signup.php POST created a new account (correlate with MantisBT user_create audit) and that mantisconnect.php POSTs returned HTTP 200. Check the User-Agent — SOAP libraries (PHP-SOAP, python-zeep, curl) vs a browser. 2) Contain: disable the newly-registered account, rotate the administrator's cookie_string by forcing an admin password reset (invalidates MANTIS_STRING_COOKIE), and set $g_allow_signup=OFF until patched to 2.28.4. 3) Hunt: enumerate every account created since the first malicious signup and every SOAP operation from that IP; review private issues/attachments/user-account reads for data exfiltration and check for destructive ops (project/issue deletes).
let win = 30m;
let signup = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem endswith "signup.php"
    | project SignupTime=TimeGenerated, cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "mantisconnect.php"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| join kind=inner signup on cIP
| where TimeGenerated between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + win)
| project SignupTime, SoapTime=TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csMethod, scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent
| order by SoapTime desc
APPLICATION

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval isSignup=if(like(uri_path,"%signup.php"),1,0), isSoap=if(like(uri_path,"%mantisconnect.php"),1,0)
| stats sum(isSignup) as signupHits sum(isSoap) as soapHits min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime values(uri_path) as uris by src
| where signupHits>0 AND soapHits>0
| eval spanSeconds=lastTime-firstTime

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="*signup.php" OR Web.uri_path="*account_prof_menu_page.php" OR Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php") by Web.src Web.uri_path Web.http_method

MantisBT SOAP endpoint (mantisconnect.php) high-volume POST burst — mass data exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the actions-on-objective phase of CVE-2026-47156 where an admin-impersonating client hammers the SOAP API to enumerate/exfiltrate all issues, attachments and user accounts across the 71 SOAP operations. Alerts on a single source IP exceeding a per-window POST threshold to /api/soap/mantisconnect.php with large aggregate response bytes. Rationale: Anchors on the exact SOAP endpoint URI and POST method; the >100-req/10-min threshold plus large scBytes captures the '71 SOAP operations / full data exfiltration' impact called out in the advisory. Distinct pivot from UC1 (volume/bytes vs signup correlation). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-47156/ • https://mantisbt.org/blog/archives/mantisbt/846
ATT&CKT1213 T1119
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy legitimate SOAP integration (CI bot, dashboard, mobile app) polling issues at high frequency
  • Bulk import/export migration job run by an admin via the SOAP API
  • Monitoring/synthetic health-check hitting mantisconnect.php on a tight interval
  • A misconfigured client retrying failed SOAP calls in a tight loop (check scStatus for repeated 500s)
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0") // replace with a lookup of sanctioned SOAP integration IPs; `| search NOT [| inputlookup mantis_soap_allowlist.csv | fields src]` in Splunk
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and whether it maps to a sanctioned integration; inspect scStatus distribution (many 200s + large scBytes = successful bulk pulls) and User-Agent. 2) Contain: block the IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, disable the account it authenticated as, and rotate the admin cookie_string; if the org is unpatched, take the SOAP API offline ($g_enable_soap_api / webserver rule) until 2.28.4 is deployed. 3) Hunt: quantify what was read — map SOAP calls to private issues, attachments and the user-account table (id/name/email); look for follow-on destructive operations and for the same IP reappearing against other public-facing apps.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem endswith "mantisconnect.php"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| summarize ReqCount=count(), TotalBytesOut=sum(scBytes), SuccessCount=countif(scStatus==200), UserAgents=make_set(csUserAgent,10) by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ReqCount > 100   // legit SOAP clients rarely exceed 100 ops / 10 min; mass enumeration blows past this
| order by ReqCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out dc(Web.status) as statusVariety from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php" AND Web.http_method=POST by Web.src _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

First-seen SOAP client on MantisBT mantisconnect.php (new source, post-bypass admin activity) AIExploitation Medium
Baseline anti-join surfacing source IPs that hit /api/soap/mantisconnect.php for the first time in 30 days — the shape of an attacker abusing the CVE-2026-47156 bypass to act with administrator privileges from a source that was never a legitimate SOAP integration. Prioritises new clients returning HTTP 200 with large payloads. Rationale: SOAP integrations are stable, allow-listable source IPs; a never-before-seen IP driving mantisconnect.php POSTs is the cleanest available proxy for post-bypass privileged abuse when request bodies aren't logged. Leftanti/append baseline anti-join is a distinct pivot from UC1 (correlation) and UC2 (threshold). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-47156/ • https://mantisbt.org/docs/master-1.3.x/en-US/Admin_Guide/html/admin.config.soap.html
ATT&CKT1550.004 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly-deployed or relocated legitimate SOAP integration (new server, new egress IP after cloud migration)
  • Occasional developer testing the SOAP API from a workstation
  • DHCP/NAT change putting an existing integration behind a different public IP
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the SOAP endpoint for the first time this month
Suppression filter
| where src NOT IN [| inputlookup mantis_soap_allowlist.csv | fields src] // maintain an allowlist of sanctioned SOAP integration source IPs to suppress known-good new-but-authorized clients
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the new source IP (ASN/geo/reverse DNS) and compare its User-Agent to known integrations; confirm POSTs returned 200 with non-trivial bytes. 2) Contain: if unrecognised, block at the WAF and disable any account seen authenticating from it; rotate the admin cookie_string. 3) Hunt: 30-day baseline warms this rule — during warmup, manually validate each new IP against the sanctioned-integration inventory and pivot into UC2 (volume) and UC1 (signup) for the same IP to confirm the full CVE-2026-47156 chain.
let baseline = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where csUriStem endswith "mantisconnect.php"
    | distinct cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem endswith "mantisconnect.php"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| join kind=leftanti baseline on cIP
| summarize Requests=count(), Success=countif(scStatus==200), BytesOut=sum(scBytes), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), UserAgents=make_set(csUserAgent,10) by cIP
| order by BytesOut desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where earliest=-30d latest=-1d Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php" by Web.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| stats sum(baseline) as baseline sum(recentCount) as recentCount sum(recentBytes) as recentBytes by src
| where (isnull(baseline) OR baseline=0) AND recentCount > 0
| sort - recentBytes

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval baseline=1 | fields src baseline
| append [| tstats summariesonly=false count as recentCount sum(Web.bytes_out) as recentBytes from datamodel=Web where earliest=-1d Web.uri_path="*mantisconnect.php" AND Web.http_method=POST by Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| stats sum(baseline) as baseline sum(recentCount) as recentCount sum(recentBytes) as recentBytes by src
| where (isnull(baseline) OR baseline=0) AND recentCount > 0
| sort - recentBytes

Turning threat intelligence into decisive action with Defender Experts

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-15 9 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Security teams have never had more visibility, yet rarely have they felt more uncertain. Signal pours in from endpoints, identities, cloud workloads, and a sprawling mix of third-party tools. The post Turning threat intelligence into decisive action with Defender Experts appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1528 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-15 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

TuxBot v3 Evolution, an IoT botnet framework built with LLMs. Read our analysis of its cross-compiled binaries, C2 architecture and bugs. The post TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] TuxBot Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (credential brute-force propagation) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TuxBot/Akiru known ELF sample execution and drop (SHA256 pivot) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TuxBot/Akiru IoT botnet C2 connection to known infrastructure · [LLM] TuxBot fallback C2 via digikalas.online DGA subdomains and DNS TXT queries · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TuxBot/Akiru IoT botnet C2 connection to known infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed TuxBot v3/Akiru C2 hosts (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127) and developer domain digikalas.online, including the encrypted bot-protocol ports 31337/1999 and the SSH-2.0-CNC-Control-Server management port 2222. Article-specific because these are the exact IPs/ports/domain recovered from the source tree and observed live on Xpanse. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 IPs (209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127), developer domain digikalas.online and bot-protocol ports (31337/1999/2222) from the source tree and Xpanse; corroborated by TheHackerNews and gbhackers which independently report 209.182.237.133:2222 / port 1999|31337. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html • https://gbhackers.com/llm-assisted-tuxbot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel VM deliberately sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Internal IOC-validation/BAS tooling (e.g. AttackIQ, SafeBreach) replaying these indicators
  • Firewall/IDS appliance sinkholing the domain and logging the redirect as a 'connection'
  • Shared-hosting reuse: a benign service later assigned 209.182.237.133 after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("CylanceUI.exe","safebreach-connector") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source device and the process that opened the socket (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName); confirm it is an IoT/Linux asset and whether the connection succeeded. 2) Contain: block 209.182.237.133, 185.10.68.127 and *.digikalas.online at the firewall/DNS, isolate the device from the LAN, and preserve the running binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same src for Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (UC2), DNS to digikalas.online subdomains and TXT queries (UC3), and search the fleet for the SHA256 71dfbb17… (UC4).
let c2ips = dynamic(["209.182.237.133","185.10.68.127"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has "digikalas.online"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["209.182.237.133","185.10.68.127"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (c2ips) or DestinationHostName has "digikalas.online" or RequestURL has "digikalas.online"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TuxBot Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (credential brute-force propagation) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a single host spraying outbound connections to many public destinations on the Telnet (23/2323) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) ports — the working infection vector of TuxBot's Telnet scanner (1,496 credential pairs) and ADB scanner. High-fidelity because near-zero legitimate endpoints fan out across these IoT-specific ports. Rationale: Targets TuxBot's confirmed working infection vector — the Telnet scanner (1,496 cred pairs) plus ADB (5555) scanner — via a fan-out threshold on the exact scanner ports; ports 23/2323/5555 have essentially no benign endpoint fan-out, making the volume signal high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-tuxbot-v3-iot-botnet-uses-llm-generated-code/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rumble) sweeping the estate on Telnet/ADB ports
  • Shodan-style internet-wide research scanner running from a sanctioned host
  • Network/asset-discovery tool enumerating IoT/OT gear on 23/2323
  • Mobile-device test lab legitimately probing ADB 5555 across many devices
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.0.5","10.20.0.6")   // approved vuln-scanner source IPs — replace with your scanner allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is not a sanctioned scanner (check asset inventory / scanner allowlist) and review the initiating process and destination geo-spread. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network and block egress on 23/2323/5555; if it is an unmanaged IoT device, quarantine its switch port/VLAN. 3) Hunt: check the same host for C2 to the UC1 IPs/domain and for the SHA256 71dfbb… (UC4); pull authentication logs on any internal targets it reached on port 23 for successful weak-credential logons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555)   // Telnet, alt-Telnet, Android Debug Bridge scanners
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // botnet scanner sprays thousands; >100 distinct public IoT ports/day is abnormal for one endpoint
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceVendor
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // fan-out threshold for IoT scanner behaviour
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=23 OR RemotePort=2323 OR RemotePort=5555)
| cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4, negate=true)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctTargets))
| DistinctTargets > 100
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
TuxBot fallback C2 via digikalas.online DGA subdomains and DNS TXT queries AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts TuxBot's fall-back C2 channels: DNS lookups to the developer domain digikalas.online (and algorithmically-generated subdomains like newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online) and DNS TXT queries used as a covert command channel. Article-specific because digikalas.online is the confirmed live operator domain and DNS TXT / SHA512-DGA are named fall-back mechanisms. Rationale: Keys on the confirmed live operator domain digikalas.online (resolving on Arvan Cloud) and the named SHA512-DGA / DNS-TXT fall-back channels; the leaked subdomain newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online proves the actor uses multi-label subdomains under this parent, so any resolution is high-value. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://securityonline.info/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1568.002 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign DNS TXT lookups for SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification by mail servers and security tools
  • Domain-monitoring/threat-intel platforms actively resolving digikalas.online for tracking
  • Certificate/ACME validation issuing TXT queries at scale
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection crawlers enumerating the parent domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("named","dnsmasq","systemd-resolved") and RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate the two signals — any hit on digikalas.online is high-priority; for raw TXT queries, filter out mail servers and confirm the querying process is not a mail/security service. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block digikalas.online and its subdomains at the resolver and isolate any endpoint that resolved it. 3) Hunt: correlate the client IP with UC1 C2 connections and UC2 scanner fan-out; if beaconing intervals appear, capture and decode the TXT responses for encoded commands and pivot on any new resolved IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".digikalas.online")[0])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, Subdomain, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "digikalas.online" or QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), QueryTypes = make_set(QueryTypeName), DistinctNames = dcount(Name), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by ClientIP, Name
| order by Queries desc

TuxBot/Akiru known ELF sample execution and drop (SHA256 pivot) AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of the confirmed TuxBot v3 Evolution debug sample (SHA256 71dfbb17…), the x86_64 build with symbols submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20. Article-specific single-hash pivot for the recovered bot binary, including its habit of hiding under a dot-prefixed filename. Rationale: Single confirmed IOC — the SHA256 71dfbb17…, the x86_64 debug build submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20; an exact-hash match is unambiguous and the union covers both drop (FileWritten) and execution. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or reverse-engineer detonating the known sample in a managed sandbox
  • EDR/AV telemetry from a quarantine or research VLAN where the sample is retained for study
  • Threat-intel platform hashing an archived copy during an automated enrichment sweep
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned analysis VM; capture the full path (watch for a dot-prefixed hidden filename) and the parent process that dropped/launched it. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill and quarantine the binary, and preserve it plus any persistence entries for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for sibling GCC 14.2.0 production builds; pivot the host onto UC1 (C2 IPs/domain), UC2 (scanner fan-out) and UC3 (DGA/TXT DNS) to scope the infection stage.
let badhash = "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d";
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
