Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.

OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task maintaining reverse SSH tunnel forwarding RDP AIInstallation High
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot's persistence: a scheduled task named 'Apple Sync' that re-establishes a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding the local RDP (3389) port to the attacker every hour. Also catches the ssh.exe reverse-forward (-R ... 3389) invocation itself. Both are unique to this campaign's back-connection stage. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim task name 'Apple Sync' (article code block) plus the ssh reverse-forward of RDP/3389 described in the back-connection stage — both are campaign-unique. Cross-checked against Kaspersky press release and The Hacker News write-up confirming the SSH-tunnel/RDP mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1572 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DevOps/SRE reverse SSH tunnels for jump-host access
  • IT tooling that schedules ssh port-forwards for remote support
  • A sysadmin genuinely naming a task 'Apple Sync' for iCloud/Apple sync (rare on Windows servers)
  • Bastion/tunnel software (autossh) creating -R forwards to internal hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("autossh.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bastion","jumphost"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks/ssh command line and the InitiatingProcess chain; confirm the -R forward target is an external/attacker IP and the local port is 3389. Check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat and a newly-created RDP user. 2) Contain: delete the 'Apple Sync' task, kill ssh.exe, block the remote tunnel IP at the firewall, and disable/network-isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep for termsrv.dll modification, HDUtil.exe, extl.exe, and additions to 'Remote Desktop Users' across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "Apple Sync")
     or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R" and ProcessCommandLine has "3389")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "Apple Sync")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-R" and CommandLine has "3389")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot termsrv.dll patch enabling concurrent RDP sessions AIInstallation High
Hunts OkoBot's replacement of the legitimate C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll with a patched copy that permits multiple concurrent RDP sessions. Flags any write/modify/delete of termsrv.dll by a process other than the Windows servicing stack (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker/msiexec). Rationale: Uses the verbatim termsrv.dll code block and the article's explicit description of replacing the legitimate DLL with a patched one for multi-RDP. Excluding the servicing stack (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker/poqexec) removes the only legitimate writers, so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/quality update replacing termsrv.dll via TrustedInstaller (excluded)
  • Legit RDP-wrapper / concurrent-session tools used intentionally by IT (RDPWrap)
  • Backup/restore or system-image tooling rewriting System32
  • Antivirus quarantine/restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "WinSxS")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the new termsrv.dll hash/signature against the Microsoft-shipped version for the OS build; identify the writing process and its parent. 2) Contain: restore the clean termsrv.dll from WinSxS/backup, kill the writer, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Apple Sync' task, new local RDP users, firewall RDP allow rules, and inbound RDP logons (4624 type 10) around the modification time.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","msiexec.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","msiexec.exe","poqexec.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OkoBot termsrv.dll Patch for Concurrent RDP Sessions

OkoBot HDUtil launcher execution (target/nouac) with HWID guardrail AIInstallation High
Hunts the OkoBot HDUtil launcher, a VMProtect-obfuscated module the SSH bot uses to deploy payloads via its 'target' command (with optional 'nouac'/'noattach'/'user=' and enumeration commands 'enumsessions'/'enumadapters'). HDUtil gates execution on %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat, so hwid.dat file activity is a corroborating signal. Rationale: Anchored on the launcher binary name HDUtil.exe and its exact command verbs (target, nouac, noattach, enumsessions, enumadapters) from the article's command table, plus the %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat HWID guardrail. These strings are wholly campaign-specific and won't collide with commodity tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1480 T1027 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate utility coincidentally named HDUtil.exe (verify signer/path)
  • Hard-drive vendor tooling with 'HDUtil' branding running benign commands
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • Backup/imaging software passing a 'target' argument (verify the binary is HDUtil.exe specifically)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Seagate","Western Digital","Microsoft") and FolderPath has "Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the HDUtil.exe signer/path is not a known vendor tool, capture the SHA256, and check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat and the payload named after 'target' (e.g. extl.exe). 2) Contain: kill HDUtil.exe and its children, quarantine the binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (SSH bot / TeviRAT), search the fleet for HDUtil.exe and hwid.dat, and review recent SFTP/SSH tunnel connections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("target","nouac","noattach","enumsessions","enumadapters") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("target","nouac")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\HDUtil.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\HDUtil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("target","nouac","noattach","enumsessions","enumadapters")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot UAC bypass via auto-elevated msconfig.exe spawning payload AIExploitation Medium
Hunts OkoBot's HDUtil 'nouac' UAC bypass, which abuses Windows RPC and the auto-elevating msconfig.exe (Project Zero 2019 technique) to run a payload at High integrity without a UAC prompt. Flags msconfig.exe spawning a non-standard, elevated child process. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit statement that HDUtil's 'nouac' option bypasses UAC via Windows RPC and auto-elevated msconfig.exe. msconfig.exe rarely spawns arbitrary elevated children, so a High/System-integrity child of msconfig.exe is a strong (if noisier) escalation signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1548.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin launching a tool from the msconfig 'Tools' tab (Event Viewer, Command Prompt, etc.)
  • Legitimate troubleshooting where msconfig is used to launch system utilities
  • Software installers that call msconfig for boot configuration
  • Endpoint management scripts interacting with System Configuration
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Windows\\System32\\","\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\") and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the msconfig grandparent chain — was msconfig itself launched by explorer/user, or by a script/SSH-bot context? Check whether the child is a signed system tool or an unknown binary in a temp/ProgramData path. 2) Contain: if the child is unsigned/untrusted, kill it, quarantine, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with HDUtil.exe target/nouac executions and hwid.dat on the same host, and review for follow-on payloads (extl.exe, keylogger, stealer).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msconfig.exe"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("High","System")
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","msconfig.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\msconfig.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\WerFault.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OkoBot UAC Bypass via Auto-Elevated msconfig.exe

OkoBot browser-extension loader extl.exe deployed via HDUtil AIInstallation High
Hunts OkoBot's first SFTP-delivered module: extl.exe, the browser-extensions loader (the injector chain that sideloads Rilide-style crypto-theft extensions), executed via '.\HDUtil.exe target extl.exe'. Detects extl.exe execution and its HDUtil parentage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim invocation '.\HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' and the module name extl.exe from the Browser-extensions-loader section. The HDUtil→extl.exe parent-child pair is a distinctive, high-fidelity pivot unique to OkoBot. Ledger/Trezor extension-injection objective corroborated by The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated internal tool named extl.exe (verify path/signer/hash)
  • Developer build artifact abbreviated 'extl' (check parentage — should NOT be HDUtil.exe)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
  • Browser enterprise-extension deployment tooling (parent is a management agent, not HDUtil.exe)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture extl.exe SHA256 and confirm the parent is HDUtil.exe or a script chain; inspect Chromium 'User Data\*\Extensions' and Local State/Secure Preferences for newly-added unpacked/unsigned extensions. 2) Contain: kill extl.exe, remove the injected extension(s), reset affected browser profiles, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to SeedHunter/keylogger/stealer modules and check crypto-wallet apps (Ledger Live, Trezor Suite) and browser wallet extensions for tampering.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "extl.exe" or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "extl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\extl.exe" or (ParentProcessName endswith "\\HDUtil.exe" and CommandLine has "extl")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot RDP back-connection: local RDP user creation + firewall opening AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot enabling attacker RDP access: adding a user to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, opening firewall ports for inbound RDP, and flipping fDenyTSConnections to 0. Any one of these on an endpoint outside a change window is suspicious; together they map the back-connection sequence. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's back-connection steps: create a user in the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, open firewall ports for inbound RDP, and enable RDP (fDenyTSConnections). Bundling the three complementary commands raises fidelity while each remains article-grounded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1021.001 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk enabling RDP for legitimate remote support
  • GPO/Intune baselines toggling fDenyTSConnections or RDP firewall rules
  • New admin onboarding added to Remote Desktop Users
  • RMM tooling opening 3389 during provisioning
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","mmc.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/parent — legitimate config comes from GPO/Intune/admin sessions; OkoBot comes from an SSH-bot/script chain. Enumerate any newly-added RDP user and its creation time. 2) Contain: remove the rogue account, close the firewall rule, restore fDenyTSConnections=1, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with the 'Apple Sync' task, termsrv.dll modification, and inbound RDP logons (4624 type 10) from external IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "localgroup" and ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and ProcessCommandLine has "/add")
     or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "3389")
     or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop")
     or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\net.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net1.exe") and CommandLine has "localgroup" and CommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and CommandLine has "/add"
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\netsh.exe" and CommandLine has "advfirewall" and (CommandLine has "3389" or CommandLine has "Remote Desktop"))
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot disabling Windows Defender notifications via registry AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot suppressing Defender alerts to enable stealthy module delivery, done via a registry modification. Detects setting DisableNotifications/DisableEnhancedNotifications under Windows Defender Security Center by a non-installer process. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the SSH bot 'disables Windows Defender notifications via a registry modification' before delivering modules. Scoping to the Defender Security Center Notifications keys with a value of 1 and excluding installer/GPO writers keeps this targeted. Falcon left empty — FDR's registry telemetry (AsepValueUpdate) only covers autostart keys, not this notification value. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise GPO/Intune policy disabling Defender toast notifications org-wide
  • MDM baseline hardening that suppresses Security Center pop-ups
  • Third-party AV installer taking over Defender and muting notifications
  • Admin manually reducing notification noise on a jump box
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("intune","CCM","SCCM"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process — policy comes from gpscript/msiexec/MDM; OkoBot comes from an SSH-bot/script chain or an unsigned binary. Check timing against any legitimate policy push. 2) Contain: revert the value, re-enable Defender notifications, and isolate the host if the writer is untrusted. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on OkoBot activity on the same host — HDUtil.exe, extl.exe, 'Apple Sync' task, termsrv.dll patch, and SFTP module delivery.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender Security Center\Notifications" or RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableNotifications","DisableEnhancedNotifications")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","gpscript.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender Security Center\Notifications" or RegistryValue in~ ("DisableNotifications","DisableEnhancedNotifications")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","gpscript.exe","MsMpEng.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts upload endpoint: path-traversal sequence in multipart filename AIExploitation Medium
Hunts authenticated POSTs to FacturaScripts /api/3/uploadfiles or /api/3/attachedfiles where the request carries directory-traversal sequences (../, ..%2f, ..%5c) — the article's exact primitive for escaping MyFiles/ via the unsanitized getClientOriginalName() filename. Article-specific because legitimate FacturaScripts uploads never contain traversal syntax in the client filename. Rationale: Uses the article's named sinks (/api/3/uploadfiles, /api/3/attachedfiles) plus the ../ traversal signature that escapes MyFiles/. Note the traversal lives in the multipart Content-Disposition filename, not the URL — reliable only where a WAF/proxy inspects the body (CommonSecurityLog) or access logs capture request bodies; hence the companion file-write UCs. Defender XDR has no web-access-log table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Burp/Acunetix) probing the FacturaScripts upload endpoints with traversal payloads
  • Authorized pentest engagement replaying this exact GHSA PoC
  • WAF false-positive matching literal '..' in a benign filename such as 'report..final.pdf'
  • Backup/sync tooling posting archive paths containing relative segments
Suppression filter
| where user!="" and NOT match(coalesce(http_user_agent,""),"(?i)(nessus|acunetix|nuclei|burp|zgrab|nmap)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the alerting SourceIP — confirm the multipart filename contains ../ and identify the authenticated user/API token; check the HTTP response code (2xx = write likely succeeded). 2) Contain: revoke the offending API token/session and block the SourceIP at the WAF; snapshot Dinamic/Assets/ and node_modules/ for forensics before cleanup. 3) Hunt: pivot to the file-write and .htaccess-chain UCs on the same host/time window; enumerate any .php/.phtml/.htaccess written under Dinamic/Assets or node_modules and any subsequent GET to those paths returning PHP-executed output.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles") or Message has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles")
| where RequestURL has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","..\\") or Message has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","Path Traversal","directory traversal")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts: PHP/.htaccess web-shell written into web-served Dinamic/Assets or node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write outcome of the traversal: the web-server user creating a PHP-family file or an .htaccess override inside Dinamic/Assets/ or node_modules/ — the two directories the shipped htaccess-sample excludes from index.php rewriting, so Apache serves them directly. These paths should never receive attacker-controlled executable content in normal operation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact web-served directories (Dinamic/Assets, node_modules) combined with the BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS-bypassing extensions (.htaccess plus php-family) and a web-server initiating process. A PHP or .htaccess file appearing in these asset dirs written by httpd/php/nginx is the traversal primitive landing on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FacturaScripts plugin install/update writing bundled PHP assets into Dinamic/
  • npm install/build repopulating node_modules with vendored .php or .htaccess sample files
  • Deployment/CI pipeline syncing application code into the web root
  • Developer manually copying a debugging PHP file into an assets folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","git.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","composer install","git checkout"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file's content and hash (SHA256) — confirm it is PHP code or an AddType/AddHandler .htaccess rather than a benign asset; note the InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, take the web app offline or drop a Deny-from-all rule over Dinamic/Assets, and rotate the web-server user's credentials/API tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the upload-endpoint UC for the originating request, look for a second dropped payload plus subsequent inbound GETs to the file path, and scan the whole web root for other newly-created php/htaccess files by the same process.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")

| extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
| where Ext in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","htaccess")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd.exe","apache.exe","apache2","httpd","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, Ext, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

FacturaScripts RCE chain: .htaccess handler-remap override plus payload drop in same asset dir AIExploitation High
Detects the article's Step-3 code-execution chain on the endpoint: an attacker-written .htaccess (remapping a benign extension to the PHP handler) landing in Dinamic/Assets or node_modules, immediately followed by a second file (the payload) in the same web-served directory. The .htaccess override in these Apache-direct-served folders is essentially never legitimate and is the linchpin that turns arbitrary write into RCE. Rationale: Chains the two writes the advisory's Step 3 spells out (upload .htaccess with AddType application/x-httpd-php, then upload x.png payload) into a single temporal correlation within a web-served asset dir — far higher fidelity than either write alone. The Falcon variant isolates the .htaccess override linchpin that uniquely enables the extension remap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • FacturaScripts/plugin installer laying down a directory-level .htaccess alongside static files
  • CI artifact extraction writing an .htaccess and multiple assets together
  • Admin manually hardening an asset directory by dropping a Deny .htaccess next to existing files
Suppression filter

Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .htaccess contents (look for AddType/AddHandler/SetHandler mapping a non-PHP extension to php) and inspect the paired payload file for PHP code; capture the initiating web-server account. 2) Contain: delete both files, take the site offline or override the directory with Deny-from-all, and rotate the web-server user credentials and any upload-capable API tokens. 3) Hunt: review web logs for inbound GETs to the payload path (successful RCE trigger), check for outbound C2 from the web-server process, and sweep the entire document root for other .htaccess overrides written by the same process.

TidGi Desktop wiki worker spawning a command interpreter (TiddlyWiki startup-module RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: after a malicious TiddlyWiki repo is imported, an auto-registered `module-type: startup` tiddler executes `require('child_process').execSync(...)` inside the TidGi Node.js wiki-worker thread, spawning a shell/LOLBin. A knowledge-management wiki app spawning cmd/powershell is anomalous and directly evidences exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit mechanics from the advisory (startup-module auto-exec calling require('child_process').execSync inside the TidGi wiki-worker) — a wiki app parenting cmd/powershell/LOLBins is high-fidelity. Cross-checked DeepWiki (worker-thread architecture runs in-process, so InitiatingProcess=TidGi.exe) and MITRE T1218.015. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3.1-wiki-worker-and-nodejs-tiddlywiki • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/015/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1218.015
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki owner running their own PoC/security test of the advisory
  • A legitimately-installed TiddlyWiki plugin that intentionally shells out to a system tool
  • TidGi feature that opens an external file/URL via a helper that transits cmd.exe
  • Unrelated node.exe located in a folder path coincidentally containing the string 'TidGi'
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","--git-dir","rev-parse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and TidGi's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; benign hits are usually git/backup helpers (excluded) — attacker payloads show execSync-style `cmd /c` with attacker commands. Identify the workspace folder and the most recently added tiddlers/*.js.tid file. 2) Contain: kill the TidGi and child process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the imported wiki workspace directory to prevent re-boot re-execution. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on child processes, outbound connections from TidGi.exe, and any git.exe clone that delivered the repo; check other users who imported the same repo/URL.

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","calc.exe")

Malicious startup-module tiddler (.js.tid) written into a TiddlyWiki tiddlers/ directory AIDelivery Low
Hunts the delivery artifact of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: import of a malicious repo drops a JavaScript module tiddler (title like `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` → file `$__plugins__poc__startup.js.tid`) into the wiki's `tiddlers/` directory, which TidGi auto-loads and registers as an executable module at boot. Surfaces newly written `.js.tid` module tiddlers for content triage (check for `module-type: startup`). Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete on-disk artifact (tiddler title `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` serialised as a `.js.tid` file under `tiddlers/`) and the git-clone/TidGi/node writer of the import. File telemetry can't see `module-type: startup` content, so this is a triage hunt — pair with UC1 for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3-wiki-management-system

  • User cloning/opening their own trusted wiki repository

  • Developer authoring a legitimate JS widget/macro tiddler in their workspace
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged .js.tid file and check the tiddler header for `module-type: startup` (or `module-type: filteroperator`/`macro`) and `type: application/javascript` with a `text` body calling require/child_process/exec — benign plugin tiddlers rarely do. Note the workspace and whether a git clone immediately preceded the write. 2) Contain: if the body invokes shell/`child_process`, quarantine the workspace directory before TidGi next boots it and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (TidGi spawning a shell) on the same host/time; identify the source repo URL/folder and any other endpoints that imported it.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "\\tiddlers\\"
| where FileName endswith ".js.tid"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "\\tiddlers\\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js.tid"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

n8n-MCP cross-tenant workflow version read/enumeration via n8n_workflow_versions (CVE-2026-54052) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts high fan-out use of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in list/rollback mode within a single host/session, the read path an authenticated tenant abuses to pull other tenants' un-isolated version snapshots (which embed node credential references and auth headers). Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable MCP tool name and its read modes rather than generic API abuse. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable tool name `n8n_workflow_versions` and its read modes (list/rollback) confirmed in n8n-mcp docs, plus the tenant_id session parameter used by multi-tenant HTTP mode; fan-out threshold turns legitimate single-workflow use into an enumeration signal. Splunk uses a raw app-log search because n8n-mcp stdout has no native CIM datamodel home. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1526 T1078 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate AI agent (Claude/Cursor/Windsurf) doing a bulk workflow audit or cleanup across many workflows in one session
  • Scheduled version-retention job iterating history to prune old snapshots
  • The one-time 2.56.1 upgrade migration touching all existing history
  • Platform admin performing a genuine multi-workflow restore/rollback
  • Monitoring/health-check that periodically lists versions
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName !has "migration" and Sample !has "retention" and Sample !has "scheduled-prune"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending host/session's raw n8n-mcp log lines; extract the acting tenant_id and the distinct workflow_ids/tenant_ids read — confirm whether the read tenant_id matches the owner tenant of each workflow. 2) Contain: if reads cross tenant boundaries, apply the advisory workaround immediately — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions in the server env (Docker .env) and restart, or fail over each tenant to its own instance/DB; then upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: for every foreign workflow_id touched, treat the embedded node credentials/auth headers as exposed — rotate them, and search the same logs for follow-on delete/prune/truncate (see companion UC).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"list"','"mode":"rollback"','mode=list','mode=rollback')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize DistinctWorkflows = dcount(WorkflowId), Reads = count(), TenantIds = make_set(TenantId, 10), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctWorkflows > 20   // 20 = fan-out ceiling; a legit AI agent rarely reads >20 distinct workflow version histories per host/hour
| order by DistinctWorkflows desc
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"list\"" OR "\"mode\":\"rollback\"" OR "mode=list" OR "mode=rollback")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(workflow_id) as distinct_workflows count as reads values(tenant_id) as tenant_ids min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen by host, _time
| where distinct_workflows > 20
| sort - distinct_workflows
n8n-MCP destructive workflow version backup deletion (delete/prune/truncate) — CVE-2026-54052 impact AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on invocation of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in delete/prune/truncate mode, the integrity/availability path an authenticated tenant abuses to destroy other tenants' un-isolated version backups. Article-specific: matches the exact tool name and its destructive modes rather than a generic file-delete pattern. Rationale: Matches the exact `n8n_workflow_versions` tool plus its three destructive modes (delete/prune/truncate confirmed in n8n-mcp docs) — the article explicitly states an authenticated tenant 'could delete or destroy other tenants' stored backups.' Destructive modes are rare enough to alert on; the query surfaces tenant_id/workflow_id so an analyst can immediately test cross-tenant ownership. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate retention maintenance using prune/truncate (normal housekeeping modes)
  • The 2.56.1 upgrade migration which intentionally clears previously un-scoped backups
  • Admin manually rolling back a bad version then deleting it
  • CI/CD redeploy pipeline that resets workflow version history
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "migration" and SyslogMessage !has "scheduled" and ProcessName !has "retention"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the acting tenant_id and target workflow_id from the log line; verify whether the deleting tenant owns that workflow — a mismatch is a confirmed cross-tenant destruction. 2) Contain: disable the tool now (DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions), restart the server, and restore affected version history from DB/offsite backup; upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same tenant_id for prior list/rollback reads (recon before destruction) and treat any node credentials in the destroyed/read snapshots as compromised — rotate them.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"delete"','"mode":"prune"','"mode":"truncate"','mode=delete','mode=prune','mode=truncate')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, TenantId, WorkflowId, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n-MCP Destructive Workflow Version Backup Operation (CVE-2026-54052)
id: b3e1c7a2-4f8d-4a1e-9c3b-7d2e5f0a9c14
status: experimental
description: Detects invocation of the n8n-mcp n8n_workflow_versions tool in a destructive mode (delete/prune/truncate), the impact path of CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant backup destruction in multi-tenant HTTP deployments.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j6r7-6fhx-77wx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1565.001
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  product: n8n_mcp
  service: application
detection:
  selection_tool:
    message|contains: 'n8n_workflow_versions'
  selection_mode:
    message|contains:
      - '"mode":"delete"'
      - '"mode":"prune"'
      - '"mode":"truncate"'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_mode
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate version-retention pruning
  - The 2.56.1 upgrade migration that clears un-scoped backups
level: high
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"delete\"" OR "\"mode\":\"prune\"" OR "\"mode\":\"truncate\"" OR "mode=delete" OR "mode=prune" OR "mode=truncate")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| table _time, host, source, tenant_id, workflow_id, _raw
| sort - _time
n8n-MCP vulnerable multi-tenant config exposure (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT without version-tool mitigation) AIExploitation Low
Config-audit hunt: flags n8n-mcp instances running in multi-tenant HTTP mode (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true) where the n8n_workflow_versions tool is NOT disabled and the build is at or below the vulnerable 2.56.0 — the exact preconditions for CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant access. Article-specific because it keys on the named env vars, tool name, and fixed version from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the three concrete advisory facts — env var `ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true`, the `DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions` mitigation string, and the fixed version boundary 2.56.0/2.56.1 — to surface exploitable instances before abuse. Low confidence because it assumes the server emits config/version in its startup logs; pair with a config-inventory check where available. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Instance flagged multi-tenant but actually serving a single tenant (advisory says single-tenant HTTP is not affected)
  • Dev/test instance intentionally multi-tenant and not internet-exposed
  • Already-patched 2.56.1 host still echoing the env flag (version filter should exclude it, but startup log ordering may split the strings)
  • Instances where the version string isn't logged, causing an isnull() catch-all match
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "single-tenant" and HostName !has "dev" and HostName !has "test" and HostName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host is genuinely multi-tenant (>1 tenant/token served) and reachable by tenants — cross-check against the config-inventory/orchestration manifest. 2) Contain: for exposed vulnerable instances, apply a workaround now — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions, or restrict the HTTP endpoint to trusted operators, then schedule the 2.56.1 upgrade (its migration isolates and clears un-scoped backups). 3) Hunt: on any instance that was vulnerable, replay the two companion detections (cross-tenant reads, destructive deletions) over the full exposure window to determine whether the gap was actually abused.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n-mcp" or SyslogMessage has "n8n_mcp"
| where SyslogMessage has "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" and SyslogMessage has_any ("true","enabled")
| extend Version = extract(@'(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Mitigated = iif(SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions', true, false)
| extend Parts = split(Version, ".")
| extend VulnVersion = iif(isnotempty(Version) and (toint(Parts[0]) < 2 or (toint(Parts[0]) == 2 and (toint(Parts[1]) < 56 or (toint(Parts[1]) == 56 and toint(Parts[2]) <= 0)))), true, false)
| where Mitigated == false and (VulnVersion == true or isempty(Version))
| summarize Version = any(Version), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" ("true" OR "enabled")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(?<ver>\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
| eval mitigated=if(match(_raw,"(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions"),1,0)
| eval vuln_version=if(isnotnull(ver) AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))<2 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))==2 AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))<56 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))==56 AND tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),2))<=0)))),1,0)
| where mitigated=0 AND (vuln_version=1 OR isnull(ver))
| stats latest(ver) as version, latest(_raw) as sample, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen by host, source
| sort - last_seen

Anyquery server mode bound to all interfaces (exposed unauthenticated MySQL port) AIDelivery High
Hunts for the Anyquery binary launched in `server` mode with a wildcard bind (0.0.0.0), which exposes the unauthenticated MySQL-compatible port abused in CVE-2026-50006 for ATTACH DATABASE arbitrary file write. Surfaces the attack-surface exposure before any exploitation occurs. Rationale: Uses the article's exact invocation `anyquery server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8070`; the combination of the named binary, the `server` subcommand and a wildcard bind is the precise exposure precondition for the CVE and is not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx • https://github.com/julien040/anyquery/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data/analytics team legitimately running Anyquery server on an internal, network-segmented host
  • Container image that binds 0.0.0.0 by convention but is only reachable inside a private overlay network
  • Developer running `anyquery server` in a local test/CI environment
  • Reverse-proxy fronted deployment where 0.0.0.0 bind is intentional but auth is enforced upstream
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Anyquery version (`anyquery --version`); anything < 0.4.5 is vulnerable. Check the bind address and whether the port is reachable from outside the host/subnet. 2) Contain: firewall the listener to localhost/trusted CIDRs or stop the service; upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceFileEvents for anyquery-initiated writes to /etc/cron.d, /var/www, /root/.ssh (see the AFW use case) and inbound connections from public IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0", "--host=0.0.0.0", "-h 0.0.0.0", "0.0.0.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "anyquery"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound connection to Anyquery listener from a public IP AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for external (public-IP) network connections accepted by the Anyquery process, indicating an internet-reachable, unauthenticated MySQL-compatible endpoint is being reached by outside clients — the delivery vector for the CVE-2026-50006 ATTACH DATABASE write. Rationale: Ties the accepted inbound connection directly to the `anyquery` process (InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName) with a public remote peer, matching the article's 'unauthenticated attackers connecting to the MySQL-compatible server port'. Sentinel/Datadog left empty because inbound-accept events with process attribution are not present in the ASIM network or standard Datadog Linux schemas (explained per prompt guidance). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate BI/reporting clients connecting to an intentionally public Anyquery endpoint
  • Cloud provider health-check probes hitting the exposed port
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching the port without exploitation
  • VPN-exit / NAT gateway making internal client traffic appear as a single public IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate/reputation-check the RemoteIP and count distinct source IPs; a spray of unique public IPs suggests mass scanning. 2) Contain: restrict the listener to trusted source ranges and upgrade to Anyquery >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: for any RemoteIP of interest, pivot to DeviceFileEvents for anyquery writes to persistence paths and to DeviceProcessEvents for downstream cron/webshell reverse shells within the following minutes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/anyquery$/i
| ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=anyquery All_Traffic.direction=inbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app

Anyquery process writing files to cron/webroot/SSH persistence paths (ATTACH DATABASE AFW) AIInstallation High
Highest-fidelity detection for CVE-2026-50006: the Anyquery process itself creating files under cron directories, web roots, or SSH key paths. ATTACH DATABASE materialises a SQLite file at the attacker-chosen path, so a write by anyquery into /etc/cron.d, /var/spool/cron, /var/www, or /root/.ssh is a direct exploitation signal. Rationale: Combines the article's exact write targets (/etc/cron.d/pwn, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/www/html/shell.php, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys) with the initiating process being anyquery — a database-federation tool that has no legitimate reason to write into cron/webroot/SSH. Datadog omitted because auditd file-target-path is not in the standard Datadog Linux schema. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/restore tooling copying an Anyquery .db into /var/www or a home directory
  • Sysadmin manually redirecting Anyquery output to a file under an atypical path
  • Anyquery legitimately configured with its data directory pointed at a shared web-served folder
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) running as the anyquery service account writing crontab entries
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/var/www" and FileName endswith ".db" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--datadir")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file — a valid SQLite header (`SQLite format 3`) followed by cron/PHP/SSH-key text confirms the ATTACH DATABASE abuse. Note the target path and owning UID. 2) Contain: delete the malicious file, kill the anyquery process, isolate the host, and upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: check cron execution and web/PHP process trees for the injected reverse-shell payload and review /root/.ssh/authorized_keys for attacker keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh") or FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anyquery"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh", "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
